pasos.1.titulo: Get the data and plot it
pasos.1.texto: Download the table or print the graph paper, and draw the light curve: days on the horizontal axis, magnitude on the vertical one. Careful! The magnitude axis is upside down: smaller numbers go at the top, because they are the brighter ones. Use band g (green light).
pasos.2.texto: Look at your plot: the supernova gets brighter and brighter for about two weeks and then fades. Find the highest point of your curve — the brightest one — and write down its magnitude.
pasos.3.titulo: Measure Δm15 and enter your values
pasos.3.texto: Count 15 days to the right of the peak and read the magnitude at that point of your curve. Δm15 is the difference between that magnitude and the peak one. Type the two numbers you measured here.
pasos.4.texto: Δm15 tells us how much light it really gave off. Comparing that with how bright it looks gives the distance.
pasos.5.texto: Let's see how close you got to the distance astronomers measure.
resultado.luminosidad: Light it really gave off (absolute magnitude)
resultado.comparar: Astronomers measure {d} Mpc using the redshift.
resultado.excelente: Excellent! You are very close to the real value.
resultado.bien: Very good! That is the typical accuracy of this technique.
resultado.revisa: It is worth checking the peak: a difference like this usually comes from misreading the brightest point.
resultado.explica_dif: It is never exact, and that is fine: galaxies also move on their own, which shifts the result a little.

estampillas.science_ayuda: That night's photo: you can see the galaxy and, on top of it, the supernova.

estampillas.difference_ayuda: Subtracting the two makes the galaxy vanish, leaving only what is new: the supernova. That is why the galaxy's light does not spoil the measurement.

cuaderno.vaciar_confirmar: This will delete your {n} results. Press again to confirm.

cierre.texto: Mark each supernova as a point: the true distance on the horizontal axis, the distance you worked out on the vertical one. Both axes have the same scale, so if your method were perfect every point would land exactly on a diagonal line.
cierre.p1: Do your points roughly follow a straight line? What does that mean?
cierre.p2: Did nearly all of them end up above the diagonal, nearly all below, or spread on both sides? If they are all on the same side, something you are measuring is consistently a little off.
cierre.p3: Which supernova came out worst? Go and look at its light curve: did it have few points, or a gap right near the peak?
cierre.p4: Astronomers used exactly this idea to discover that the universe is expanding faster and faster, and won the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics for it. What would you add to your measurement to trust it more?
cierre.imprimir: Print my table and the graph paper
cierre.papel_alt: Graph paper for plotting the distance you worked out against the true distance.
cierre.faltan: You do not have enough results to plot yet.
pasos.6.titulo: Do it again with another supernova
pasos.6.texto: Your result is already recorded above, under “My results”. Go back to the list and measure another one: with four or more you will be able to plot them all together and see whether the method really works.
esquema.titulo: What are we going to measure?
esquema.p1: A Type Ia supernova gets brighter and brighter for about three weeks, reaches a peak and then slowly fades. That picture of brightness against time is called a light curve, and it is what you are going to draw from the real data.
esquema.p2: Three things come out of the curve: the day it was brightest, t(peak); how bright it got, m(peak); and Δm15, the amount of magnitude it lost in the 15 days after the peak. Δm15 measures how fast it fades.
esquema.p3: What is it for? All Type Ia supernovae explode in very much the same way, so they give off almost the same amount of light. If we know how much light it really gave off and we measure how much reaches us, we can work out how far away it is: just as if you knew every light bulb was identical and guessed how far one was from how faint it looks.
esquema.p4: Δm15 refines the idea: the ones that fade more slowly are a little more luminous. That is why it is worth measuring.
metodo.intro: This section is for you, not for the class. It explains why the activity works: how the measured brightness relates to distance, and why astronomers talk about a 'distance modulus' instead of talking about megaparsecs directly.
metodo.s1_p1: A supernova emits a certain amount of energy per second. That is its luminosity, L, and it is a property of the supernova itself: it does not depend on where we are.
metodo.s1_p2: That light leaves in all directions. Once it has travelled a distance d, all of that energy is spread over the surface of a sphere of radius d, whose area is 4πd². What a telescope measures is not L but the flux: the energy arriving each second on each square metre of the mirror.
metodo.s1_p3: Hence the inverse square law: at twice the distance the same light spreads over four times the area and the flux drops to a quarter; at three times, to a ninth. This is all the underlying physics the activity needs. The rest is how to write it in the units astronomers use.
metodo.s2_titulo: 2. Astronomers do not measure flux, they measure magnitudes
metodo.s2_p1: The magnitude scale comes from ancient Greece: the brightest stars were 'first magnitude' and the faintest visible to the naked eye were sixth. When flux could finally be measured properly, the old scale was kept and pinned to a precise definition:
metodo.s2_p2: That is where the two oddities you need to warn the class about come from. First: the scale runs backwards, because of the minus sign — a smaller number means brighter. Second: it is logarithmic, not linear. A difference of 5 magnitudes is exactly a factor of 100 in flux, so one magnitude is a factor of 2.512 (the fifth root of 100).
metodo.s3_p1: The apparent magnitude m is what we see from Earth, and it mixes two things together: how much light the object emits and how far away it is. A powerful distant supernova can look just like a faint nearby one.
metodo.s3_p2: To separate them, the absolute magnitude M is defined: the magnitude the object would have if it were 10 parsecs away. It is a convention, but a useful one, because M depends only on L. M is intrinsic luminosity written in magnitudes.
metodo.s4_titulo: 4. The distance modulus: the central idea
metodo.s4_p1: Let us write both magnitudes with the same formula. The apparent one uses the flux arriving from the real distance d; the absolute one, the flux that would arrive from 10 parsecs:
metodo.s4_formula1:
m = −2.5 · log₁₀( L / (4πd²) ) + C
M = −2.5 · log₁₀( L / (4π(10 pc)²) ) + C
metodo.s4_p2: Subtracting them is where it gets interesting: the luminosity L and the constant C cancel, and so does the 4π. Only the distance is left:
metodo.s4_formula2: μ ≡ m − M = 5 · log₁₀( d / 10 pc )
metodo.s4_p3: That difference is called the distance modulus, μ. And here is the point worth being clear about before walking into class: μ is not an intermediate step towards the distance — μ IS the distance, written in magnitudes instead of megaparsecs. The relation inverts without losing anything:
metodo.s4_p4: So measuring the distance modulus and measuring the distance are the same operation. Every 5 magnitudes of μ means multiplying the distance by 10:
metodo.s4_p5: The supernovae in the catalogue sit between μ ≈ {mu_min} and μ ≈ {mu_max}, that is, between about {d_min} and {d_max} Mpc.
metodo.s5_titulo: 5. The problem: M cannot be measured
metodo.s5_p1: Since μ = m − M, getting the distance needs both magnitudes. The apparent one, m, is measured directly: that is what the telescope does, and it is what the class will read off the plot. The absolute one, M, is not: knowing it would mean knowing in advance how much light the object emits, which is exactly what we do not know.
metodo.s5_p2: Unless the object is a standard candle: a class of object whose luminosity we know from its physics, without measuring it case by case. That is what closes the argument.
metodo.s6_titulo: 6. Why Type Ia supernovae work as standard candles
metodo.s6_p1: A Type Ia is a white dwarf that pulls material from a companion star until it approaches the Chandrasekhar limit, around 1.4 solar masses. Because they all explode on reaching practically the same mass, they release almost the same energy: M_B ≈ −19.3 for all of them.
metodo.s6_p2: That is what makes the activity possible. You measure m from the plot, assume M = −19.3, and the subtraction gives μ, which is the distance. That is exactly the path the class follows.
metodo.s7_titulo: 7. The Phillips relation: from 'almost identical' to 'correctable'
metodo.s7_p1: 'Almost the same energy' is not 'the same'. Used as a pure candle, Type Ia supernovae have a scatter of about 0.3-0.4 magnitudes, which translates into a 15-20 % error in distance.
metodo.s7_p2: Phillips found in 1993 that this residual is not random: supernovae that fade more slowly are intrinsically more luminous. Δm15 — how many magnitudes it drops in the 15 days after maximum — measures that speed, and allows a correction:
metodo.s7_p3: With the correction the scatter falls to about 0.15 magnitudes, close to 7 % in distance. That is why the teacher panel shows both numbers: the one the class gets with the pure standard candle, and the corrected one. The gap between them is, in miniature, the leap observational cosmology made in the 1990s.
metodo.s8_p1: Distances and redshifts for many supernovae build the Hubble diagram. At moderate distances the relation is nearly linear, d ≈ cz/H₀, and fitting it gives the Hubble constant: the expansion rate of the universe. The class's final exercise — plotting estimated distance against true distance — is a simplified version of that diagram.
metodo.s8_p2: In 1998, two independent teams took this same technique to far more distant supernovae and found they looked fainter than expected: they were further away than a decelerating universe predicted. Dark energy and accelerating expansion came out of that, and the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics. The chain of reasoning the class follows is the same one; only the distance and the precision change.
metodo.s9_p1: ZTF observes in the g band, but the Phillips relation is defined in the B band. The conversion was calibrated with 1500 synthetic SALT2 supernovae, measured with the same code the app uses, so the fit absorbs our own estimator's biases. Galactic extinction along the line of sight is also subtracted.
metodo.s9_p2: On those simulations, where the answer is known exactly, the full chain recovers the distance with a −3 % bias and 4 % scatter. On the real catalogue supernovae, the median difference against Hubble's law is 7 %. It is worth telling the class that this residual is not a flaw in the method: galaxies also move on their own, and that peculiar velocity contaminates the reference distance.
